# 9.3 Neural Networks and CNNs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a neural network is

A **neural network** is a type of machine learning modelled after the human brain, using interconnected nodes to learn through trial and error.

Its structure is built from **nodes**, the basic processing units, which form layers that process different levels of detail in data.

## Example 1: a college acceptance model

The inputs are grades and class activities. The hidden layers each take on a level of detail — the first layer focuses on grades, for example English and Maths grades.

Each node processes a specific aspect within its layer, with dense connections to all nodes in the next layer. The "dense" connection is what lets a later layer combine every aspect the previous layer worked out, rather than following a single chain.

## Example 2: a temperature conversion model

The simple case is a linear conversion from °C to °F, with one input (°C) and one output (°F). The model computes:

$$\text{Output} = \text{Weight} \times \text{Input} + \text{Bias}$$

Training is a matter of correcting the weight and bias. Initial, incorrect weights might give:

$$F = 5.67 \times C + 12.5$$

and the refined weights:

$$F = 1.828 \times C + 28.54$$

**Complexity warning:** using more nodes — for example cubic equations — can overcomplicate simple linear problems. This connects directly to the model fitting parameters: the number of nodes increases model complexity, and more complexity is not automatically better.

## The convolution operation

**Convolution** is a mathematical operation combining two functions, for example input data and a kernel, to generate an output. It is widely used in signal processing and computer vision.

A **kernel**, for example a $3 \times 3$ matrix, slides over the input data, performing element-wise multiplication and summation to produce a new feature matrix.

## Convolutional Neural Networks

**Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)** are feed-forward neural networks that learn feature engineering via filter (kernel) optimisation. In other words, the kernels are not designed by hand — the network works out what they should be.

A key layer is the **convolution layer**, which applies kernels to extract features.

## CNNs in computer vision

Digital photos are represented as pixel arrays, with RGB values from 0 to 255. That numeric representation is what makes convolution possible on an image at all.

One application of convolution is **blurring**, where the kernel replaces pixels with the mean of their neighbours.

A cat classification pipeline runs:

```text
Input → [Conv → ReLU → MaxPool] → [Conv → ReLU → MaxPool] → Fully Connected → Output
```

The convolution-and-pooling block appears twice, each repetition working on the features the previous one extracted, and the fully connected layer at the end turns those features into the final output.

| **Node** | The basic processing unit of a neural network; nodes form layers that process different levels of detail in data |

| **Blurring** | A convolution application in which the kernel replaces pixels with the mean of their neighbours |

# 1 Computer Category and Programming Language

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two categories of computer

Every computer falls into one of two categories, and the dividing line is how much of its behaviour is fixed in advance.

A **special-purpose computer** is a computer designed for a particular function. It executes the same stored set of instructions whenever it is requested to run, so it does one job and does not need to be told how to do anything else. Microwave ovens, washing machines and medical diagnostic equipment all contain special-purpose computers.

A **general-purpose computer** is used for solving many different types of problems. It is available in various sizes and has a wide range of capabilities. Because it is not tied to a single stored routine, the same machine can be given a new set of instructions and made to do something new — which is exactly what programming is for.

## Classes of general-purpose computer

General-purpose computers are classified by size and by the scale of work they are built to handle.

| Class | Description | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Microcomputers** | Sometimes referred to as personal computers (PCs) | Individual and general use |
| **Laptop (notebook) computers** | The smallest microcomputers | Portable personal use |
| **Desktop computers** | Compact microcomputer systems that fit on a desk, designed for individual use | Individual use |
| **Workstations** | The largest type of microcomputer | Scientific and engineering applications |
| **Mainframe computers** | The largest computer; massive memory and extremely rapid processing power | Large-scale business, military and scientific fields |
| **Supercomputers** | Built for tasks requiring rapid and complex calculations involving numerous variables | Scientific research, weather prediction, aircraft design, nuclear weapons |

Mainframes are described as handling massive amounts of data or complex processes, which is why they belong in large-scale business, military and scientific settings rather than on a desk. Supercomputers are distinguished not by the volume of data but by the speed and complexity of the calculation, which is why the examples are all problems with numerous interacting variables.

## Machine language

**Machine language** is the natural language of the computer. It is the only language that can be directly used by a computer, so it does not need translation and is executed immediately. Every instruction is a binary string of 1s and 0s.

The advantage follows from that directness: machine language runs fast and efficiently, because nothing stands between the instruction and the hardware. The disadvantages follow from it too. Programs written in binary strings are difficult to write and debug, and each computer has its own machine language, so machine language is **not portable** — a program written for one type of computer cannot be run on another type.

## Assembly language

**Assembly language** consists of English-like abbreviations in place of raw binary. This makes it far easier to read than machine language, but the trade-off is that assembly programs cannot be directly processed by the computer. They must be translated first.

An **assembler** is a language translator that converts assembly language into machine code. The full path is:

```text
Assembly Language --> Assembler + Linker --> Machine Language
```

Because of variations in assembly languages between machines, programs written using them are also not portable. Assembly language is useful for implementing system hardware and for small embedded system applications. Its advantages are that the programmer is in control of the hardware, and that the resulting code is space and time efficient.

## High-level languages

**High-level languages** — Basic, Java and FORTRAN, for example — are **machine independent**. Programmers do not need to know anything about the internal structure of the computer, and they deal with high-level coding rather than with hardware detail.

High-level languages enable programmers to write instructions using English words and familiar mathematical symbols and expressions. As with assembly, the price of readability is translation:

```text
High-Level Language --> Compiler or Interpreter --> Machine Code --> Hardware
```

Notice the pattern across all three levels. The closer a language sits to the hardware, the faster and more controlled it is but the harder it is to write and the less portable it becomes; the further from the hardware, the more readable and portable, but the more translation the machine must do first.

## Keywords

|---|---|
| **Special-purpose computer** | A computer designed for a particular function, which executes the same stored set of instructions when requested |
| **General-purpose computer** | A computer used for solving many different types of problems, available in various sizes and with a wide range of capabilities |
| **Microcomputer** | A general-purpose computer sometimes referred to as a personal computer (PC) |
| **Laptop (notebook) computer** | The smallest microcomputer |
| **Desktop computer** | A compact microcomputer system that fits on a desk, designed for individual use |
| **Workstation** | The largest type of microcomputer, used in scientific and engineering applications |
| **Mainframe computer** | The largest computer, with massive memory and extremely rapid processing power, used to handle massive amounts of data or complex processes |
| **Supercomputer** | A computer used for tasks requiring rapid and complex calculations involving numerous variables |
| **Machine language** | The natural language of the computer; the only language that can be directly used by a computer, written as binary strings of 1s and 0s |
| **Assembly language** | A language consisting of English-like abbreviations, which cannot be directly processed by the computer |
| **Assembler** | A language translator that converts assembly language to machine code |
| **High-level language** | A machine-independent language, such as Basic, Java or FORTRAN, written using English words and familiar mathematical symbols and expressions |
| **Portability** | The property of a program being able to run on a type of computer other than the one it was written for |

# 2 Programming Intro

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Hardware, software and the user

A computer system can be pictured as three layers:

```text
User --> Software --> Hardware
```

**Hardware** only understands the binary system, which is machine language. That is hard for humans to understand and use directly, so something has to sit in between.

**Software** is that interface between humans and hardware. It is a set of step-by-step instructions for hardware operations. Its job runs in both directions: it translates human intention into a form computers can understand, and it turns feedback from the hardware into a form humans can understand.

## Programming

**Computer programming** is the process of writing, testing, debugging and maintaining the source code of computer programs. Programming is done through software development, and through programming we create software. The point of it is practical: we use programming to solve hard or large-scale problems that would not be tractable by hand.

## Computational thinking

**Computational thinking** involves the ability to:

- think procedurally — to break a task into ordered steps;
- think logically — to reason about conditions and outcomes;
- think ahead — to anticipate what the program will need.

## Two ways to run code

There are two ways to run Python code, and they suit different situations.

| | Interactive mode | Script mode |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt | Has the `>>>` prompt | Does not have the `>>>` prompt |
| Getting a result | Result returned immediately after pressing enter | File must be created and saved before executing the code to get results |
| Editing | No direct method to edit code | A direct way of editing your code |
| File | — | Uses a `.py` file |

Interactive mode starts with `>>>` and answers straight away, which makes it good for trying a single expression. Script mode stores the code in a file, which is what makes editing possible — the code still exists after it has run.

## Indentation

**Indentation** is space at the beginning of a code line. What it means depends on the language, and this is a genuine difference rather than a matter of taste:

- In **Python**, indentation marks out a block of code. It is part of the syntax.
- In **other programming languages**, indentation is for readability only and carries no specific meaning.

## The print() function

The `print()` function is used to print values to the screen. When Python calls the `print()` function, a value is passed to the function. A value passed to a function call is called an **argument**.

```python
print('Hello, world!')
```

The keyword `end` defines something to be printed automatically at the end of the output. It defaults to the newline character `\n`, which is why each `print()` normally starts a fresh line.

```python
print('Hello', end='')
print('world')
```

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hardware** | The physical layer of a computer, which only understands the binary system (machine language) |
| **Software** | The interface between humans and hardware: step-by-step instructions for hardware operations, translating human intention into a form computers can understand and hardware feedback into a form humans can understand |
| **Computer programming** | The process of writing, testing, debugging and maintaining the source code of computer programs |
| **Computational thinking** | The ability to think procedurally, think logically and think ahead |
| **Interactive mode** | A way of running code with the `>>>` prompt, in which the result is returned immediately after pressing enter |
| **Script mode** | A way of running code using a `.py` file, in which the file must be created and saved before executing the code to get results |
| **Indentation** | Space at the beginning of a code line; in Python it marks a block of code, in other languages it only aids readability |
| **Argument** | A value passed to a function call |
| **end** | A keyword of `print()` that defines something to be printed automatically at the end of the output; it defaults to the newline `\n` |

# 3 Variables and Data Types

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## String concatenation

The **concatenation operator** `+` is used to join two strings together as the operation.

```python
>>> 'hello' + ' python'
'hello python'
```

## The input() function

The `input()` function reads a string from standard input. Whatever the user types, `input()` returns it as the **string** type — so a number typed at the keyboard arrives as text, not as a number, until it is converted.

```python
name = input('What is your name? ')
```

## Variables

**Variables** are containers for storing data values. You store a numerical or data value into a variable temporarily and get the value from the variable later when you need it. A variable is created at the moment you assign a value to it.

Variables are worth using for four reasons:

- they make code more readable;
- they let you avoid typing a value repeatedly;
- they make code easier to modify and debug, because a value appears in one place rather than many;
- they let programs run faster, since a stored value does not have to be recomputed.

## Naming rules

A variable name must obey these rules:

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| Contains only letters, numbers and underscores (`_`) | No other characters |
| Does not start with a number | `8piece` is invalid |
| No spaces | — |
| Case sensitive | `AGE`, `age` and `Age` are three different variables |
| Does not use reserved keywords | See the list below |

The **reserved keywords** cannot be used as variable names:

```python
['False', 'None', 'True', 'and', 'as', 'assert', 'async', 'await',
 'break', 'class', 'continue', 'def', 'del', 'elif', 'else', 'except',
 'finally', 'for', 'from', 'global', 'if', 'import', 'in', 'is',
 'lambda', 'nonlocal', 'not', 'or', 'pass', 'raise', 'return', 'try',
 'while', 'with', 'yield']
```

Beyond the rules, names should be short and descriptive. **Camel case naming** makes compound names more readable: `myOneMethod` is easier to read than `myonemethod`.

## Assigning variables

The equal operator `=` is used to assign a value to a variable. Python also allows **multiple assignment**, assigning in a single statement.

Assigning a single value to multiple variables:

```python
>>> x = y = z = 50
```

Assigning multiple values to multiple variables:

```python
>>> a, b, c = 5, 10, 15
```

## Data types

| Type | Holds | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Integer** | Whole numbers | `0`, `-2`, `29` |
| **Float** | Floating point numbers | `1.0`, `9.902`, `1e10`, `44e-2` |
| **String** | Textual values | `'the'`, `'1'`, `'num of line'` |

Note that `'1'` is a string, not an integer. The quotation marks, not the character inside them, decide the type — which is why input read with `input()` has to be converted before it can be used in arithmetic.

## Keywords

|---|---|
| **Concatenation operator (`+`)** | The operator used to concatenate two strings as the operation |
| **input()** | A function that reads a string from standard input and returns the string type |
| **Variable** | A container for storing data values, created when you assign a value to it |
| **Camel case naming** | A naming style that makes compound names more readable, such as `myOneMethod` |
| **Multiple assignment** | Assigning a value to multiple variables in a single statement |

| **String** | A data type for textual values such as `'the'`, `'1'`, `'num of line'` |

An **expression** consists of values (such as `4`) and operators (such as `*`). The defining property of an expression is that it always evaluates down to a single value.

```python
14
```

That single-value rule is what lets expressions be nested inside one another: because every expression collapses to one value, an expression can stand anywhere a value can.

All Python programs can call a basic set of functions called the **built-in functions**, which include `print()` and `input()`. These need nothing to be set up first — they are always available.

## Importing modules

Python also comes with a set of modules called the **standard library**. Each **module** contains a related group of functions that can be embedded in your programs.

A module is brought in with the `import` statement:

```python
>>> import math
```

After you import a module, you can use all the functions of that module. The `math` module, imported above, is the standard library module for mathematical functions.

# 5 Lists

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a list is

A **list** is a collection of items in a particular order. Square brackets `[]` indicate a list, and the individual elements are separated by commas.

```python
numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

The phrase "in a particular order" is what makes the rest of this lesson work: because the order is fixed, each element has a permanent position that can be used to reach it.

## Index

You can access any element in a list by telling Python the position, or **index**, of the desired item. Access an element by writing the name of the list followed by the index of the item enclosed in square brackets.

The first item's index is `0`.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> numList[0]
0
>>> numList[2]
2
```

## The len() function

The `len()` function returns the number of elements in a list.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> len(numList)
6
```

Because indexing starts at 0, a list of length 6 has indexes 0 to 5 — the last valid index is always one less than the length.

## Adding elements to a list

The `append()` method adds the new element to the end of the list.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> numList.append(12)
>>> numList
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12]
```

You can add a new element at any position in your list by using the `insert()` method. The first argument is the index at which the new element should sit; everything from that position onwards shifts along.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> numList.insert(2, 12)
>>> numList
[0, 1, 12, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

## Removing elements from a list

Which tool you use depends on what you know about the item.

Use the `del` statement when you know the **position** of the item you want to remove from a list.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> del numList[2]
>>> numList
[0, 1, 3, 4, 5]
```

Use the `remove()` method if you only know the **value** of the item you want to remove. It deletes only the first occurrence of the value you specify — a point worth remembering when a value appears more than once:

```python
>>> numList = [1, 5, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3]
>>> numList.remove(3)
>>> numList
[1, 5, 4, 2, 0, 3]
```

The second `3` survives, because only the first occurrence was removed.

## Finding the index of an element

`lst.index(value)` returns the first occurrence of the value.

```python
>>> numList = [1, 5, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3]
>>> numList.index(3)
4
```

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **List** | A collection of items in a particular order, written with square brackets `[]` and elements separated by commas |
| **Index** | The position of an element in a list, used to access it; the first item's index is 0 |
| **len()** | A function that returns the number of elements in a list |
| **append()** | A method that adds a new element to the end of the list |
| **insert()** | A method that adds a new element at any position in a list |
| **del** | A statement used to remove an item from a list when you know its position |
| **remove()** | A method used to remove an item when you only know its value; it deletes only the first occurrence |
| **index()** | A method that returns the first occurrence of a value in a list |

# 6 For-loop

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Purpose

A **for loop** is used to iterate a block of statements several times. Rather than writing the same statements once for each item you want to handle, you write them once and let the loop present each item in turn.

## Syntax

```python
for variable in someList:
    statements
```

The loop variable takes the value of each element of the list in order, and the indented statements run once for each of those values. The indentation is what marks out the block that belongs to the loop.

```python
numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
for n in numList:
    print(n)
```

## Converting each element

A list read in from input holds strings, so the loop body is the natural place to convert each element to `int` or `float` before using it in arithmetic.

```python
for item in someList:
    value = int(item)
    print(value * 2)
```

```python
for variable in range(start, stop, step):
```

```python
for i in range(10):
```

```python
import random
```

# 8 If Statement

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Boolean values

**Boolean values** have only two possible values: `True` or `False`. Every condition a program tests eventually reduces to one of these two.

```python
'5' + '6' == '56'   # evaluates to True
1 != '1'            # evaluates to True
8 >= 8              # evaluates to True
```

In the first example the `+` concatenates the two strings into `'56'`, and that result is then compared with `'56'`, so the whole expression is `True`. The arithmetic-looking part happens before the comparison.

The second example is worth pausing on: the integer `1` and the string `'1'` are not equal, so `!=` gives `True`. A comparison looks at type as well as at the characters on the page.

## Relational operators

**Relational operators** compare two values and produce a Boolean.

| Operator | Description | Example | Evaluates to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<` | Less than | `2**3 < 9` | `True` |
| `>` | Greater than | `0 > 1` | `False` |
| `<=` | Less than or equal to | `4 <= 5` | `True` |
| `>=` | Greater than or equal to | `9**0.5 >= 3` | `True` |
| `==` | Equal to | `1 == 2` | `False` |
| `!=` | Not equal to | `'B' != 'B'` | `False` |

Note the distinction between `=` and `==`. A single `=` assigns a value to a variable; a double `==` asks whether two values are equal.

## The if statement

```python
if condition:
    statements
```

The statements run only when the condition evaluates to `True`. The colon and the indentation together mark out the block that the condition guards.

```python
ph = float(input('Enter the pH level: '))
if ph < 7.0:
    print(str(ph), 'is acidic.')
if ph > 7.0:
    print(str(ph), 'is alkaline.')
```

Here two independent `if` statements are used. Each is tested on its own, and a pH of exactly 7.0 satisfies neither, so nothing is printed.

## The if … else … statement

```python
if condition:
    statements1
else:
    statements2
```

`else` catches everything the condition did not, so exactly one of the two blocks always runs.

```python
n = int(input())
line = 'Today, I ate ' + str(n) + ' apple'
if n > 1:
    line += 's.'
else:
    line += '.'
print(line)
```

The example shows the pattern at its most useful: a sentence is assembled up to the point where it depends on the data, and the branch supplies only the part that differs.

## The if … elif … else … statement

```python
if condition1:
    statements1
elif condition2:
    statements2
else:
    statements3
```

`elif` is tested only if the condition above it was `False`, so the conditions are checked in order and the first one that succeeds wins.

```python
age = int(input('What is your age? '))
if age < 11:
    print('You are a kid.')
elif age < 20:
    print('You are a teenager.')
else:
    print('You are an adult.')
```

The second condition is written as `age < 20`, not as a range between 11 and 20, precisely because it is only reached when `age < 11` has already failed. The order of the branches is doing part of the work.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Boolean value** | A value with only two possibilities: `True` or `False` |
| **Relational operator** | An operator that compares two values and evaluates to a Boolean: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=` |
| **if statement** | A statement that runs its block of statements when a condition is true |
| **else** | The clause that runs when the `if` condition is false |
| **elif** | A further condition tested only when the conditions above it are false |

# 9 Boolean Operators

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three Boolean operators

Relational operators produce Boolean values; **Boolean operators** combine them. There are three types: `not`, `and`, `or`.

A **truth table** shows all possible results of a Boolean operator. Since each Boolean input has only two values, the tables are short and can be memorised outright.

## Truth table of the and operator

The `and` operator evaluates an expression to `True` if both Boolean values are `True`; otherwise it evaluates to `False`.

| Expression | Evaluates to |
|---|---|
| `True and True` | `True` |
| `True and False` | `False` |
| `False and True` | `False` |
| `False and False` | `False` |

## Truth table of the or operator

The `or` operator evaluates an expression to `True` if either of the two Boolean values is `True`; otherwise it evaluates to `False`.

| Expression | Evaluates to |
|---|---|
| `True or True` | `True` |
| `True or False` | `True` |
| `False or True` | `True` |
| `False or False` | `False` |

## Truth table of the not operator

The `not` operator evaluates to the opposite Boolean value.

| Expression | Evaluates to |
|---|---|
| `not True` | `False` |
| `not False` | `True` |

## Precedence

Operator precedence among the Boolean operators follows this order:

```text
() > not > and > or
```

Brackets are evaluated first, then `not`, then `and`, then `or`. This is why an expression such as `False and True or True` is `True`: the `and` binds tighter, so it is read as `(False and True) or True`.

A longer illustration, with the grouping made explicit by brackets:

```python
(a > b and c > d) or (a > b and a != c) or (not b == c)
```

Each bracketed group settles to a single Boolean, and the two `or` operators then combine those three results.

## Worked Boolean expressions

These expressions evaluate to `True`:

```python
2 >= 2 and 1 < 3
1 <= 2 or 1 != 1
not 'A' == 'a'
```

These expressions evaluate to `False`:

```python
not 1 == 1
'a' == 'A' or 'b' == 'B'
3 > 4 and 3 < 5
```

The last one is a common trap: `3 < 5` is perfectly true, but `and` requires both sides, and `3 > 4` is false.

## Remainder

The remainder operator `%` returns the remainder after dividing the first operand by the second operand.

```python
22 % 5                      # 2
math.floor(123 / 10) % 10   # 2
```

The second example is a digit-extraction idiom: dividing by 10 and taking the floor throws away the last digit, and `% 10` then keeps the last digit of what remains — here, the tens digit of 123.

## Integer division

Integer division `//` returns the floor value of the quotient produced by dividing the two operands.

```python
(1234 // 100) % 10          # 2
```

Because the result is the **floor**, negative operands do not simply truncate towards zero. Consider `-14 // 3`: the quotient is $-4.\overline{6}$, and the floor of that is $-5$, not $-4$.

The same reasoning settles `-13 % 3`. Since `-13 // 3` is $-5$, the remainder must be $-13 - 3 \times (-5) = 2$. The remainder is positive even though the dividend is negative, because the floor was taken downwards.

## Precedence of common operators

| Operator | Description |
|---|---|
| `**` | Exponentiation (raise to the power) |
| `*` `/` `%` `//` | Multiply, divide, modulo, and integer division |
| `+` `-` | Addition and subtraction |
| `<=` `<` `>` `>=` `!=` `==` | Relational operators |
| `not` `and` `or` | Boolean operators |

The table is ordered from highest precedence at the top to lowest at the bottom. Arithmetic happens before comparison, and comparison happens before the Boolean operators — which is why `2 + 2 == 4` needs no brackets to work as intended.

## Exercise

Evaluate the following Boolean expressions.

```python
'T' == 't' or 4 > 1
13 % 5 > 3 and not 3 == 2
(3 * 5) % (12 / 2) >= 9 ** (1 / 2)
9 > 3 * 3 or not 11 - 5 < 6 and 2 + 5 >= 7
2 + 2 == 4 and not 2 + 2 == 5 and 2 * 2 == 2 + 2
not 2 > 1 and 3 < 4 or 5 > 5 and 2 > 1 and 3 >= 3
```

Working through them using the precedence table:

| Expression | Reasoning | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `'T' == 't' or 4 > 1` | `False or True` | `True` |
| `13 % 5 > 3 and not 3 == 2` | `13 % 5` is 3, so `3 > 3` is `False`; `False and True` | `False` |
| `(3 * 5) % (12 / 2) >= 9 ** (1 / 2)` | `15 % 6.0` is `3.0`; `9 ** 0.5` is `3.0`; `3.0 >= 3.0` | `True` |
| `9 > 3 * 3 or not 11 - 5 < 6 and 2 + 5 >= 7` | `9 > 9` is `False`; `6 < 6` is `False` so `not` gives `True`; `7 >= 7` is `True`; `False or (True and True)` | `True` |
| `2 + 2 == 4 and not 2 + 2 == 5 and 2 * 2 == 2 + 2` | All three parts are `True` | `True` |
| `not 2 > 1 and 3 < 4 or 5 > 5 and 2 > 1 and 3 >= 3` | `not True` is `False`, so the first `and` group is `False`; `5 > 5` is `False`, so the second group is `False`; `False or False` | `False` |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Boolean operator** | One of the three operators `not`, `and`, `or` that combine Boolean values |
| **Truth table** | A table showing all possible results of a Boolean operator |
| **and** | Evaluates an expression to `True` if both Boolean values are `True`; otherwise `False` |
| **or** | Evaluates an expression to `True` if either of the two Boolean values is `True`; otherwise `False` |
| **not** | Evaluates to the opposite Boolean value |
| **Remainder (`%`)** | Returns the remainder after dividing the first operand by the second operand |
| **Integer division (`//`)** | Returns the floor value of the quotient produced by dividing the two operands |

# 10 Number System

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Positional notation

Ask how many numbers are in 943 and the answer depends on reading each digit together with the column it sits in:

$$943 = 900 + 40 + 3 = 9 \times 10^2 + 4 \times 10^1 + 3 \times 10^0$$

This is called **positional notation**. Written as a formula with the digits left unknown, and with $R$ standing for the base:

$$d_n \times R^{n-1} + d_{n-1} \times R^{n-2} + \dots + d_2 \times R + d_1$$

Everything else in this lesson is this one formula with a different value of $R$.

## The decimal number system

The **decimal system** is a positional system that uses 10 digits (0–9) to represent numbers. Its base is $R = 10$, so the column values are the powers of 10.

## The binary number system

The **binary system** is widely used in computer science. Its base is $R = 2$, so the column values are the powers of 2.

Each 0 or 1 is called a **bit** (binary digit).

## Bits and bytes

$$1\ \text{byte} = 8\ \text{bits}$$
$$1\ \text{KiB} = 1024\ \text{bytes}$$
$$1\ \text{MiB} = 1024\ \text{KiB}$$

Since 1 MiB is 1024 KiB and each KiB is 1024 bytes, one MiB is $1024 \times 1024 = 1\,048\,576$ bytes.

## Binary to decimal

The equivalent decimal representation of a binary number is the sum of the powers of 2 which each digit represents. For example, the binary number 100101 is converted as follows:

$$100101_2 = [1 \times 2^5] + [0 \times 2^4] + [0 \times 2^3] + [1 \times 2^2] + [0 \times 2^1] + [1 \times 2^0]$$
$$100101_2 = [1 \times 32] + [0 \times 16] + [0 \times 8] + [1 \times 4] + [0 \times 2] + [1 \times 1]$$
$$100101_2 = 37_{10}$$

The same method converts 10011101B:

$$10011101_2 = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 157_{10}$$

## Decimal to binary

To go the other way, divide repeatedly by 2 and collect the **remainders**. Converting 23:

| Dividend | Divisor | Quotient | Remainder |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23 | 2 | 11 | 1 |
| 11 | 2 | 5 | 1 |
| 5 | 2 | 2 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| 1 | 2 | 0 | 1 |

Reading the remainders from the bottom upwards gives the result **10111B**. Checking with the positional formula confirms it:

$$1 \times 2^4 + 0 \times 2^3 + 1 \times 2^2 + 1 \times 2^1 + 1 \times 2^0 = 23$$

The same procedure applied to 89:

```text
89 / 2 = 44 remainder 1
44 / 2 = 22 remainder 0
22 / 2 = 11 remainder 0
11 / 2 = 5  remainder 1
 5 / 2 = 2  remainder 1
 2 / 2 = 1  remainder 0
 1 / 2 = 0  remainder 1
```

Result: **1011001B**.

The remainders come out least significant bit first, which is why the answer is read upwards rather than downwards.

## Hexadecimal notation

**Hexadecimal** notation is based on 16, so $R = 16$ and each column is a power of 16. The digits run 0–9 and then A–F for the values 10 to 15.

| Hexadecimal | Decimal |
|---|---|
| `1A` | 26 |
| `FF` | 255 |

`1A` is $1 \times 16 + 10 = 26$, and `FF` is $15 \times 16 + 15 = 255$ — the largest value two hexadecimal digits can hold, and also the largest value one byte can hold. That correspondence is why hexadecimal is used for binary data: one byte is exactly two hexadecimal digits, so conversion between binary and hexadecimal is a matter of grouping bits rather than doing arithmetic.

## Base-N conversion

Decimal, binary and hexadecimal are three cases of one method, so a conversion between any two bases can be done by routing through decimal: expand the source number with the positional formula to get its decimal value, then divide repeatedly by the target base to build the answer.

Converting $12_3$ into base 8:

$$12_3 = 1 \times 3^1 + 2 \times 3^0 = 5_{10}$$

Since 5 is smaller than 8, it is a single digit in base 8, so $12_3 = 5_8$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Positional notation** | Writing a number as the sum of each digit multiplied by a power of the base, as in $943 = 9 \times 10^2 + 4 \times 10^1 + 3 \times 10^0$ |
| **Decimal number system** | A positional system that uses 10 digits (0–9) to represent numbers |
| **Binary number system** | The base-2 positional system, widely used in computer science |
| **Bit** | A binary digit; each 0 or 1 |
| **Byte** | A group of 8 bits |
| **Hexadecimal notation** | A notation based on 16 |

# 12 While-Loop

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## For loop versus while loop

For loops are suitable when the number of iterations is known in advance. A **while loop** is the alternative for when it is not: it keeps going as long as a condition holds, so the number of repetitions is decided while the program runs rather than before it starts.

## Syntax

```python
while condition:
    statements
```

The condition is tested before each pass. While it is `True`, the indented block runs again; as soon as it is `False`, the loop ends and the program moves on.

## Using a while loop for accumulation

```python
i, s = 1, 0
n = int(input('Enter n: '))
while i <= n:
    s += i
    i += 1
print(s)
```

Three things are happening, and every while loop needs all three. `s` is the **accumulator**, starting at 0 and gathering the running total. `i` is the counter, starting at 1. And `i += 1` is what eventually makes the condition `i <= n` false.

Be cautious to avoid **infinite loops**. If the line `i += 1` were left out, `i` would stay at 1 for ever, the condition `i <= n` would never become false, and the loop would never end. Anything the condition depends on must be changed somewhere inside the loop.

## Augmented assignment statements

**Augmented assignment statements** are shorthand notations for performing an operation and an assignment together.

| Shorthand | Equivalent to |
|---|---|
| `x += 2` | `x = x + 2` |
| `x -= 2` | `x = x - 2` |
| `x *= 2` | `x = x * 2` |
| `x /= 2` | `x = x / 2` |
| `x //= 2` | `x = x // 2` |
| `x %= 2` | `x = x % 2` |

Each of these takes the current value of the variable, applies the operation, and stores the result back in the same variable — which is exactly what accumulating a total and advancing a counter both require.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **While loop** | A loop that repeats its statements as long as a condition holds; suitable when the number of iterations is not known in advance |
| **For loop** | A loop suitable when the number of iterations is known in advance |
| **Infinite loop** | A loop whose condition never becomes false, so it never ends |
| **Augmented assignment statement** | A shorthand notation for performing an operation and assignment together, such as `x += 2` for `x = x + 2` |

# 13 String Manipulation I

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The strip() function

`str.strip()` returns a new string with leading and trailing whitespace characters removed. Given an argument, `str.strip(s)` removes leading and trailing occurrences of the characters in `s`.

```python
>>> '  hello  '.strip()
'hello'
>>> '---hello---'.strip('-')
'hello'
```

Note the word **returns**: `strip()` produces a new string rather than altering the original, so the result has to be stored or used.

## lstrip() and rstrip()

`str.lstrip()` removes whitespace characters from the left end of a string, and `str.rstrip()` does the same at the right end. They are the one-sided versions of `strip()`, for when only one end should be touched.

```python
>>> '  hello  '.lstrip()
'hello  '
```

## String indexing

```python
str[index]
```

Each character of a string has a position, counted from 0.

```python
str = 'Hello World!'
str[0]    # 'H'
str[4]    # 'o'
str[-1]   # '!'
```

A negative index counts back from the end, so `-1` is the last character. This saves computing the length just to reach the final character.

## The len() function

`len(str)` counts and returns the length of the string `str`.

```python
>>> len('Hello World!')
12
```

## Membership operators

The **membership operators** test whether one string occurs inside another.

| Operator | Returns |
|---|---|
| `x in s` | `True` if `x` is found in `s`, otherwise `False` |
| `x not in s` | `True` if `x` is not found in `s`, otherwise `False` |

```python
>>> '+' in '1+2'
True
```

## String slicing

Slicing takes a section of a string rather than a single character.

```python
str[start slice: end slice]
```

With `str = 'python'`:

| Slice | Result |
|---|---|
| `str[:-1]` | `'pytho'` |
| `str[-1:]` | `'n'` |
| `str[1:]` | `'ython'` |
| `str[:1]` | `'p'` |

An omitted start means "from the beginning" and an omitted end means "to the end". Comparing `str[:1]` with `str[1:]` shows the rule for where the cut falls: the character at the end index is not included in the slice, so the two together account for the whole string with nothing repeated and nothing lost.

## Input text cleaning

A typical exercise: clean a string of leading and trailing special characters, including whitespaces.

```text
Sample Input:  ----***---- I am a student in SHSID ----***------
Sample Output: I am a student in SHSID
```

Both the `-` and `*` characters and the spaces have to go from both ends, but the spaces inside the sentence must survive — which is exactly what `strip()` with an argument does, since it only works inwards from the two ends.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **strip()** | `str.strip()` returns a new string with leading and trailing whitespace characters removed; `str.strip(s)` removes leading and trailing occurrences of the characters in `s` |
| **lstrip()** | Removes whitespace characters from the left end of a string |
| **rstrip()** | Removes whitespace characters from the right end of a string |
| **String indexing** | Accessing a single character by position, written `str[index]` |
| **len()** | Counts and returns the length of a string |
| **Membership operator** | `x in s` returns `True` if `x` is found in `s`; `x not in s` returns `True` if it is not |
| **String slicing** | Taking a section of a string, written `str[start slice: end slice]` |

# 14 String Manipulation II

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The join() function

`join()` builds one string out of many pieces, with a chosen separator between them. The delimiter is the string the method is called on, and the pieces are the argument.

```python
delimiter.join(list)
delimiter.join(str)
```

`delimiter.join(list)` concatenates the strings in a list using the specified delimiter. `delimiter.join(str)` concatenates the characters in a string using the specified delimiter.

```python
>>> '-'.join(['a', 'b', 'c'])
'a-b-c'
>>> '-'.join('abc')
'a-b-c'
```

The second form works because a string is treated as its sequence of characters.

## The split() function

`str.split(delimiter)` splits a string into a list of substrings based on the delimiter. It is the inverse of `join()`: one takes a list and produces a string, the other takes a string and produces a list.

```python
>>> 'a-b-c'.split('-')
['a', 'b', 'c']
```

This is the standard way to break up a line of input into the separate values it contains, which can then be converted and used individually.

## Character-class tests

Three methods report on what kind of characters a string is made of. Each returns a Boolean, so each can be used directly as an `if` or `while` condition.

| Method | Returns `True` if |
|---|---|
| `str.isalnum()` | All characters in the string are alphanumeric |
| `str.isdigit()` | All characters are digits |
| `str.isalpha()` | All characters are alphabetic |

Each returns `False` otherwise. Note the word **all** in every case: a single character of the wrong kind makes the whole test fail, which is what makes `isdigit()` a usable check before converting a string to a number.

```python
>>> 'abc123'.isalnum()
True
>>> '123'.isdigit()
True
>>> 'abc'.isalpha()
True
```

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **join()** | `delimiter.join(list)` concatenates the strings in a list using the specified delimiter; `delimiter.join(str)` concatenates the characters in a string using the specified delimiter |
| **split()** | `str.split(delimiter)` splits a string into a list of substrings based on the delimiter |
| **isalnum()** | Returns `True` if all characters in the string are alphanumeric, otherwise `False` |
| **isdigit()** | Returns `True` if all characters are digits, otherwise `False` |
| **isalpha()** | Returns `True` if all characters are alphabetic, otherwise `False` |

# 15 Computer Colour

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three primaries of light

James Clerk Maxwell identified the three primaries of light as Red, Green and Blue. This gives the **RGB** model, written `RGB(R, G, B)`, where each of the three components takes a value from 0 to 255.

```text
RGB(255, 0, 150)
```

Young, a British physician, established the reason this works: all the colours we generate form the three spectral hues of Red, Green and Blue, and these align with the colour receptors in our eye. The model has three components rather than some other number because human vision has three kinds of receptor.

## Binary colours

Each of the three components is stored in 8 bits, so a full colour occupies **24 bits**:

```text
11111111 11111111 11111111
```

The 0–255 range and the 8 bits per component are the same fact stated twice: eight bits count from 0 to 255, and all three components at their maximum give the 24 ones above.

## Hexadecimal colour notation

The same 24 bits are usually written in hexadecimal, two digits per component:

```text
#FFFFFF
```

The `#` is needed in hex mode — it is what marks the value as a hexadecimal colour rather than an ordinary number.

## ASCII

**ASCII** descends from telegraph code and was first published in 1963. It defines 128 characters, which are represented as 7-bit integers. The two figures match: seven bits give exactly 128 distinct patterns, so the character set and the bit width fit each other with nothing spare.

## HSL, HSV and HSI

RGB is not the only way to name a colour. **HSL** and **HSV** are common cylindrical-coordinate representations of points in the RGB colour model — the same colours, described by different coordinates.

| Model | Components |
|---|---|
| **HSL** | Hue, saturation, lightness |
| **HSV** | Hue, saturation, value |
| **HSI** | Hue, saturation, intensity |

All three share hue and saturation and differ only in the third component.

## Resolution

**Resolution** is measured in **ppi** (pixels per inch). A resolution of 72 ppi is described as realistic.

Vector graphics do not rely on resolution — however, displays do. A vector image can be drawn at any size without loss, but the screen it is drawn on still has a fixed number of pixels per inch.

## Colour depth

**Colour depth** describes, for graphic files and applications, the number of distinct colours an image can contain and how many bits per pixel are used to hold them. The two are directly linked: more bits per pixel means more distinct colours available, which is the same reasoning that gave 24-bit colour its range above.

## CRT

**CRT** stands for Cathode Ray Tubes, a display technology that works using electrons.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **RGB** | The colour model built on the three primaries of light — Red, Green and Blue — written `RGB(R, G, B)` with each component from 0 to 255 |
| **ASCII** | A character encoding descended from telegraph code, first published in 1963, defining 128 characters as 7-bit integers |
| **HSL** | A cylindrical-coordinate representation of the RGB colour model using hue, saturation and lightness |
| **HSV** | A cylindrical-coordinate representation of the RGB colour model using hue, saturation and value |
| **HSI** | A cylindrical-coordinate representation using hue, saturation and intensity |
| **Resolution** | The pixel density of an image or display, measured in ppi (pixels per inch) |
| **Colour depth** | The number of distinct colours an image can contain, and the number of bits per pixel used to store them |
| **CRT** | Cathode Ray Tubes, a display technology that works using electrons |

# 21 Database Fundamentals

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Database concepts

A **database** is an organised collection of data, typically stored and accessed electronically from a computer system. Databases are managed by a **Database Management System (DBMS)**, which provides tools for data creation, manipulation and retrieval.

## Data hierarchy

Data in a database is organised in levels, each built from the one below it.

| Level | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Character** | The smallest unit of data | `'A'`, `'7'`, `'@'` |
| **Field (attribute)** | A single data category, represented as a column in a table | Name, Age |
| **Record (tuple)** | A single row in a table, representing a complete data entry | `[101, Alice, 25]` |
| **Table (relation)** | A collection of related records, organised in rows and columns | Employee table |

Fields run down the table as columns and records run across it as rows, so any single value can be located by naming one of each.

## DBMS models

| Model | Structure | Relationship type | Use case | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hierarchical** | Tree-like (parent–child) | One-to-many | Organisational charts | IBM IMS |
| **Network** | Graph-like | Many-to-many | Complex relationships | CODASYL DB |
| **Relational** | Tables (rows and columns) | Foreign keys | Most modern applications | MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle |

In the **hierarchical model**, data is organised in a tree structure with a single root. Each child has one parent, which limits flexibility but is efficient for hierarchical data — an organisational chart is exactly this shape, so it fits the model without strain.

The **network model** allows multiple parent–child relationships. This suits complex data but is harder to maintain, which is the price of dropping the one-parent restriction.

The **relational model** organises data into tables and links them with foreign keys, and it underlies most modern applications.

## SQL basics

**SQL** (Structured Query Language) is used to interact with relational databases. It supports creating, reading, updating and deleting data — the **CRUD** operations.

## Creating tables

```sql
CREATE TABLE Employee (
    EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    FirstName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    LastName VARCHAR(50),
    Salary FLOAT,
    HireDate DATE,
    DepartmentID INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (DepartmentID) REFERENCES Department(DepartmentID)
);
```

A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each record. The `FOREIGN KEY` line is what makes this a relational table rather than an isolated one: it declares that `DepartmentID` refers to a record in the `Department` table.

Common data types:

| Type | Holds | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `INT` | Whole numbers | `100`, `-5` |
| `VARCHAR(n)` | Variable-length text with a maximum length of `n` | `VARCHAR(50)` for names |

## SQL CRUD operations

| Operation | Syntax | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **SELECT** | `SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition;` | `SELECT FirstName, Salary FROM Employee WHERE DepartmentID = 3;` |
| **INSERT** | `INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values);` | `INSERT INTO Employee (EmployeeID, FirstName, Salary) VALUES (101, 'Alice', 60000);` |
| **UPDATE** | `UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition;` | `UPDATE Employee SET Salary = 65000 WHERE EmployeeID = 101;` |
| **DELETE** | `DELETE FROM table WHERE condition;` | `DELETE FROM Employee WHERE Salary < 30000;` |

`SELECT` retrieves data; use `*` to select all columns. `INSERT` adds new records, specifying columns and values.

The `WHERE` clause appears in three of the four, and it is what limits the operation to the rows that match. Its absence on `UPDATE` or `DELETE` would apply the change to every row in the table.

## Advanced SQL queries

**ORDER BY** sorts results:

```sql
SELECT FirstName, Salary FROM Employee ORDER BY Salary DESC;
```

**LIMIT** restricts the number of rows returned:

```sql
SELECT * FROM Orders LIMIT 5;
```

**Aggregate functions** summarise many rows into one value. `COUNT(*)` counts total rows, and `AVG()` averages a column. Combined with `GROUP BY`, the summary is produced once per group rather than once for the whole table:

```sql
SELECT DepartmentID, AVG(Salary) AS AvgSalary FROM Employee GROUP BY DepartmentID;
```

**JOIN** combines data from multiple tables:

```sql
SELECT Employee.FirstName, Department.DepartmentName
FROM Employee
INNER JOIN Department ON Employee.DepartmentID = Department.DepartmentID;
```

| Join type | Returns |
|---|---|
| **INNER JOIN** | Matching records from both tables |
| **LEFT JOIN** | All records from the left table and matching records from the right |
| **RIGHT JOIN** | All records from the right table and matching records from the left |

The joins differ only in what happens to rows with no match on the other side, which is why `INNER JOIN` can return fewer rows than either table contains.

**ALTER TABLE** changes the structure of an existing table:

```sql
ALTER TABLE Employee ADD COLUMN Email VARCHAR(100);
```

## Exam tip

Practise writing SQL queries — `SELECT`, `JOIN`, `GROUP BY` and `ORDER BY`.

| **DBMS (Database Management System)** | The system that manages a database, providing tools for data creation, manipulation and retrieval |

| **Hierarchical model** | A DBMS model organising data in a tree structure with a single root, where each child has one parent |
| **Network model** | A DBMS model allowing multiple parent–child relationships, suitable for complex data but harder to maintain |
| **Relational model** | A DBMS model organising data into tables of rows and columns, linked by foreign keys |
| **SQL (Structured Query Language)** | The language used to interact with relational databases |

# 22 Computer Troubleshooting

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## BIOS basics

The **BIOS** (Basic Input/Output System) is firmware that initialises hardware during the boot process and provides runtime services for operating systems. It runs before the operating system exists in memory, which is why it has to be firmware rather than ordinary software.

Its functions include performing the **POST** (Power-On Self-Test) to check hardware functionality.

To access the BIOS, press keys like **F2, F10, F12 or DEL** during startup — which key varies by manufacturer. Among the common settings are **power settings**, which control power management such as sleep modes.

## The boot process

1. **BIOS activation** — the BIOS initialises and checks hardware.
2. **POST** — tests critical components (CPU, RAM, GPU).
3. **Bootloader** — loads the operating system into RAM.
4. **OS initialisation** — loads drivers and system configurations.

The order is not arbitrary: hardware must be found and tested before anything can be loaded into it, and the operating system must be in RAM before it can load its own drivers. Knowing the sequence is what makes it possible to diagnose a failure, because the point at which booting stops narrows down where the fault lies.

## Troubleshooting boot issues

| Issue | Symptoms | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| **No boot** | Blank screen, no power | Check power supply, reseat RAM/GPU, test with minimal hardware |
| **Blue screen (BSOD)** | System crashes with error code | Boot in Safe Mode (F8), update drivers, run diagnostics such as `chkdsk` |
| **Corrupt OS** | Fails to load OS | Use recovery USB/CD, repair OS, or reinstall |
| **Slow boot** | Long loading times | Disable unnecessary startup programs, run virus scans, defragment disk |
| **Boot loop** | Restarts repeatedly | Recover the Master Boot Record (MBR), check for malware, repair OS |

Each row maps onto a stage of the boot process. A machine with a blank screen and no power has not reached POST, so the fixes are all physical. A system that crashes with an error code has got as far as loading drivers, so the fixes are about drivers and disk integrity.

## Exam tip

Memorise the boot process and the common boot issue fixes.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **BIOS (Basic Input/Output System)** | Firmware that initialises hardware during the boot process and provides runtime services for operating systems |
| **POST (Power-On Self-Test)** | The BIOS test of hardware functionality, checking critical components such as CPU, RAM and GPU |
| **Bootloader** | The stage of booting that loads the operating system into RAM |
| **BSOD (Blue Screen)** | A system crash displaying an error code |
| **Safe Mode** | A diagnostic startup mode, reached with F8, used when troubleshooting a blue screen |
| **MBR (Master Boot Record)** | The record recovered when troubleshooting a boot loop |

# 23 Information Security

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Encryption basics

**Encryption** converts plaintext into **ciphertext** to protect data. **Decryption** reverses the process.

## Types of encryption

| Type | Key usage | Algorithms | Use case |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Symmetric** | Same key for encryption and decryption | AES, DES, 3DES | Fast encryption, for example file storage |
| **Asymmetric** | Public key encrypts, private key decrypts | RSA, ECC | Secure key exchange, digital signatures |

**Symmetric encryption** uses one key for both directions. DES (Data Encryption Standard) uses a 56-bit key and is outdated.

**Asymmetric encryption** is slower but secure for key exchange. The two facts fit together: because the same key both locks and unlocks in symmetric encryption, that key has to reach the other party somehow, and asymmetric encryption is what gets it there safely. Speed is why symmetric encryption is still used for the bulk data once the key has arrived.

## The Caesar cipher

The Caesar cipher is a historical example. It shifts letters by a fixed number — with a shift of 3, A becomes D and B becomes E.

## Security protocols

**TLS/SSL** (Transport Layer Security / Secure Sockets Layer) secures communication over networks, for example HTTPS websites.

A **VPN** (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel for secure remote access. One type is **voluntary tunnelling**, in which the client initiates the connection. A VPN's encryption methods combine symmetric encryption for data transfer and asymmetric encryption for key exchange — the same division of labour set out above, applied in practice.

## Exam tip

Differentiate symmetric from asymmetric encryption, and understand the use cases of TLS/SSL and VPN.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Encryption** | Converting plaintext into ciphertext to protect data |
| **Decryption** | The reverse of encryption |
| **Symmetric encryption** | Encryption using the same key for encryption and decryption, such as AES, DES and 3DES |
| **Asymmetric encryption** | Encryption using a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt, such as RSA and ECC |
| **DES (Data Encryption Standard)** | A symmetric algorithm with a 56-bit key, now outdated |
| **Caesar cipher** | A historical cipher that shifts letters by a fixed number |

## Privacy concerns

**Personal information exposure** is the central risk: leaking photos, addresses or IDs.

**Cookies** store user data, such as login sessions and preferences. The same mechanism that makes a site convenient — remembering that you are logged in — is what leaves a record of your activity behind.

## Privacy protection

Clear browser history and cookies regularly to reduce tracking.

## Computer ethics

Computer ethics are summarised as **five NOTs and one ALWAYS**.

The five NOTs:

1. Don't harm others with malicious code, for example viruses.
2. Don't interfere with others' work, for example hacking systems.
3. Don't steal data or resources.
4. Don't use unpaid proprietary software, for example pirated software.
5. Don't appropriate others' intellectual output, for example plagiarism.

The one ALWAYS:

- Use computers with consideration and respect for others.

The five prohibitions all describe harm done through a computer to another person — to their machine, their work, their property or their ideas. The single positive rule states the principle the five are instances of.

## Exam tip

Review privacy risks such as cookies and data leaks, and memorise the five NOTs and one ALWAYS of computer ethics.

# 25 Artificial Intelligence

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## AI fundamentals

AI is divided by the breadth of what a system can do.

- **Weak AI (Narrow AI)** is designed for specific tasks.
- **Strong AI (General AI)** is theoretical human-level intelligence capable of any intellectual task.

The word **theoretical** is doing real work in that second definition: every AI system in use is weak AI, and strong AI names a capability that has not been built.

Among the key elements of AI is **processing power** — high-performance hardware such as GPUs and TPUs.

## Machine learning types

| Type | Learning method | Example application |
|---|---|---|
| **Supervised** | Uses labelled data (input–output pairs) | Spam detection, image classification |
| **Unsupervised** | Finds patterns in unlabelled data | Customer segmentation, anomaly detection |
| **Reinforcement** | Learns via rewards and penalties | Game AI, robotics |

**Supervised learning** includes **classification**, which predicts discrete categories — spam versus not spam, for instance. The labels are what make this possible: the system is shown the right answer for each training input.

**Unsupervised learning** clusters data or reduces dimensionality, for example grouping customers by behaviour. With no labels available, the structure has to be found in the data itself.

**Reinforcement learning** has an agent learn by interacting with an environment, as AlphaGo did by learning through games. Here there are neither labels nor a fixed dataset, only rewards and penalties following from what the agent does.

## Neural networks

A neural network's structure begins with the **input layer**, which receives raw data.

Training runs in **epochs**, updating the network's weights and biases using **backpropagation**.

## AI milestones

| Year | Event | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| 1950 | Turing Test proposed | Framework for evaluating AI intelligence |
| 1997 | Deep Blue defeats chess champion | AI excels in rule-based games |
| 2016 | AlphaGo defeats Go champion | AI masters complex, intuitive strategy |
| 2023 | Rise of LLMs, for example ChatGPT | Natural language processing reaches new heights |

The sequence tracks a widening of what AI can handle: first a way of judging machine intelligence at all, then victory in a game with fixed rules, then a game whose strategy is described as intuitive, then open-ended natural language.

## Exam tip

Understand the AI types — weak versus strong — and the machine learning types, and know the key neural network concepts of layers and training.

## Types of system software

**System software** is the software that runs the machine itself rather than performing a user's task. The **BIOS** is one type: it initialises hardware and starts the operating system.

## Five generations of programming languages

Programming languages are classified into five generations, ordered by how far they sit from the hardware.

| Generation | Type | Example | Characteristics |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1st (1GL)** | Machine language | Binary (0s and 1s) | Hardware-specific, error-prone |
| **2nd (2GL)** | Assembly language | `MOV`, `ADD` | Symbolic, still hardware-specific |
| **3rd (3GL)** | High-level language | C, Java, Python | Human-readable, portable |
| **4th (4GL)** | Very high-level language | SQL, MATLAB | Domain-specific, closer to human language |
| **5th (5GL)** | Natural language | AI-based query systems | Conversational, experimental |

Reading down the table, two things change together. The languages become steadily more human-readable, and they become steadily less tied to a particular machine — the first two generations are hardware-specific, and portability arrives with the third.

The later generations change direction slightly. A 4GL such as SQL is not simply a more readable 3GL; it is **domain-specific**, expressing what is wanted in the vocabulary of one problem area rather than describing a general procedure. The fifth generation is marked as experimental, so it describes a direction of travel rather than a settled category.

## Exam tip

Differentiate the types of system software, and understand the five generations of programming languages.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **System software** | Software that runs the machine itself; the BIOS is one type |
| **BIOS** | System software that initialises hardware and starts the operating system |
| **1GL (machine language)** | The first generation: binary 0s and 1s, hardware-specific and error-prone |
| **2GL (assembly language)** | The second generation: symbolic instructions such as `MOV` and `ADD`, still hardware-specific |
| **3GL (high-level language)** | The third generation: human-readable and portable languages such as C, Java and Python |
| **4GL (very high-level language)** | The fourth generation: domain-specific languages closer to human language, such as SQL and MATLAB |
| **5GL (natural language)** | The fifth generation: conversational, experimental AI-based query systems |

- Programming is the process of writing, testing, debugging, and maintaining source code to create software that instructs computers to perform specific tasks.

- Computer hardware operates using binary (0s and 1s), which is difficult for humans to use directly.
- Software acts as an interface between humans and hardware.
- Programming creates software by translating human intentions into machine-executable instructions.

**Interaction Hierarchy:** User → Software → Hardware

Steps to Solve Programming Problems

1. Define the problem clearly.

2. Plan the solution (e.g., using pseudocode or flowcharts).

3. Write the code in a programming language.

4. Test and debug the program to remove errors (bugs).

**Running Python Code**

- Interactive Mode:
- Accessed via >>> prompt (e.g., in IDLE shell).
- Executes code line-by-line immediately.
- Useful for quick tests but not for editing multi-line programs.
- Script Mode:
- Code is written in a .py file (e.g., lesson1.py).
- Must be saved before running.
- Executed via Run → Run Module (or press F5 in IDLE).
- Preferred for developing full programs.

**Basic Syntax and Concepts**

+ Addition: 2 + 2 → 4

- Subtraction: 5 - 2 → 3

* Multiplication: 3 * 5 → 15

/ Division: 22 / 8 → 2.75

** Exponentiation: 2 ** 3 → 8

Note: Python uses floating-point arithmetic, so results like 2/3 + 1 may show slight imprecision (e.g., 1.6666666666666665) due to how decimals are stored in binary.

**The** **print() Function**

- Used to display output on the screen; Accepts arguments (values passed into the function).

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science H review guide (PA). Writers: Sharon 9-3. Editor: Cathy 9-3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Variables and Data Types**

- A variable is a named container that stores a value temporarily.

- Cannot contain spaces or special characters (-, !, @, etc.).
- Case-sensitive: age, Age, and AGE are distinct.

- Camel Case: numberOfDonuts
- Snake Case: number_of_donuts (preferred in Python)
- Pascal Case: NumberOfDonuts

**Basic Data Types** **and Type Conversion Functions**

- Integer (int): whole numbers like 0, -5, 42. int(x): converts to integer (e.g., int("15") → 15).
- Float (float): decimal numbers like 3.14, -0.001. float(x): converts to float (e.g., float(2) → 2.0).
- String (str): text enclosed in quotes, e.g., "hello", "123". str(x): converts to string (e.g., str(42) → "42").

- Follows standard operator precedence: Parentheses () → Exponentiation ** → Multiplication/division * / // % → Addition/subtraction + -.

- math.pi: value of π,
- math.sqrt(x): square root,

- Indexing starts at 0: fruits[0] → "apple".
- Negative indices count from the end: fruits[-1] → "cherry".
- Modify by assignment: fruits[1] = "blueberry".

**List Methods**

- len(lst): number of elements.
- lst.append(x): adds x to the end.
- lst.insert(i, x): inserts x at index i.
- del lst[i]: removes element at index i.
- lst.remove(x): removes first occurrence of x.
- lst.index(x): returns index of first occurrence of x.
- Other useful methods: pop(), sort(), reverse(), count(), clear(), extend().

## Chapter 5 For Loop

**for Loop**

- Iterates over each item in a sequence (e.g., list, string).
- Syntax:

for variable in iterable:

statements

- Example:

numbers = input().split()

total = 0

for num in numbers:

total += int(num)

**range() Function**

- Generates sequences of integers.
- Forms:
- range(stop): 0 to stop-1,
- range(start, stop),
- range(start, stop, step).
- Examples:

for i in range(5): # 0,1,2,3,4

for i in range(1, 5): # 1,2,3,4

for i in range(10, 0, -2): # 10,8,6,4,2

- Use the random module:

import random

num = random.randint(1, 6) # inclusive range

Boolean Values and Relational Operators

- Boolean values: True or False.
- Relational operators:
- <, >, <=, >=, == (equal), != (not equal).
- Examples:
- 2 ** 3 < 9 → True,

if n > 1:

age = int(input("What is your age?"))

if age < 11:

print("kid")

print("teenager")

- and: both conditions must be True.
- or: at least one condition must be True.

**while Loop**

- Syntax:

while condition:

statements

## Chapter 10 String Manipulation

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science H review guide (PA). Writers: Sharon 9-3. Editor: Cathy 9-3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

- Strings are immutable sequences of characters.
- Created with single or double quotes: "hello", 'world'.
- Indexing: s[0], s[-1].
- Slicing: s[start:end] (end is exclusive).
- Examples:
- s[1:] → from index 1 to end,
- s[:-1] → all but last character.

**Membership and Length**

- "a" in "apple" → True.
- len(s) returns number of characters.

**Cleaning Strings**

- strip(): removes leading/trailing whitespace or specified chars.
- lstrip(), rstrip(): remove from left or right only.

s = "----***Hello***----"

print(s.strip("-*")) # "Hello"

**Case Conversion**

- s.upper(): all uppercase,
- s.lower(): all lowercase,
- s.title(): first letter of each word capitalized.

**String Testing Methods**

- s.isupper(), s.islower(), s.istitle(),
- s.isalpha() (letters only),
- s.isdigit() (digits only),
- s.isalnum() (letters + digits).

**Splitting and Joining**

- s.split(delimiter): breaks string into list.
- Default delimiter: any whitespace.
- Example: "a,b,c".split(",") → ["a","b","c"].
- delimiter.join(list): combines list into string.
- Example: "-".join(["h","e","l","l","o"]) → "h-e-l-l-o".

**Modulo and Integer Division**

- x % y: remainder after division (e.g., 22 % 5 → 2).
- x // y: floor division (e.g., 7 // 2 → 3).
- Useful for digit extraction:

(1234 // 100) % 10 # extracts hundreds digit: 2

**List Comprehension**

- Concise way to create lists:

evens = [i for i in range(5) if i % 2 == 0]

#equivalent to:

evens = []

for i in range(5):

if i % 2 == 0:

evens.append(i)

**Advanced Section Examples**

- **(Expression Parsing)**
Input a string like "8--2 5+-3". Output the fully normalized expression and its evaluated result: "8+2+5-3=12". Reconstruct the expression manually—do not use eval().
- **(List Processing)**
Read a line of integers. Remove the second largest distinct value (not the second in order). Output the remaining numbers in original order.
Sample Input: 10 3 7 3 9 5
Sample Output: 10 3 3 9 5
- **(Triangle Classification)**
Given three side lengths as floats, classify the triangle as:
- "invalid", or
- "[acute/right/obtuse] [scalene/isosceles/equilateral]"
Use tolerance 1e-9 for comparisons. Sort sides manually without built-in sort.
- **(Quadratic Solver)**
Solve ax² + bx + c = 0. Handle all cases:
- a = 0 → linear (including b = 0 → no/inf solutions)
- a ≠ 0 → compute discriminant D = b² − 4ac
Output roots rounded to two decimals, sorted if two exist. Do not use eval().
- **(Accumulation Sequence)**
Compute the sum of the first 15 terms of:
1¹ − 2² + 3³ − 4⁴ + … + (−1)ⁿ⁺¹·nⁿ
Use iterative multiplication to compute powers—do not use ** for large exponents.
- **(String Sanitization)**
Input: "### HeLLo__WoRlD123!!!@@@"
Output: "Hello World123"
Rules:
- Replace underscores with single spaces
- Keep only letters, digits, and single spaces
- Collapse multiple spaces
- Title-case each word
- Do not use strip(), replace(), or regex
- **(Digit Analysis)**
Given integers L and R (1 ≤ L ≤ R ≤ 10000), count how many numbers in [L, R] contain at least one digit '3' and one digit '7'.
Sample Input: 1 100 → Output: 2 (37, 73)
Use % and // for digit extraction—do not convert every number to a string.
- **(Pig Latin with Blends)**
Translate a word into Pig Latin:
- Vowels (a,e,i,o,u): add "yay"
- Valid blends: "sch", "scr", "shr", "sph", "spl", "spr", "squ", "str", "thr", plus all 2-letter blends from class
- Otherwise: move first consonant + "ay"
Sample: "school" → "oolschay", "string" → "ingstray"

Hints

- Expression Parsing
- Watch for consecutive signs like --, +-, or -+.
- Normalize operators before calculating.
- Use a running total to build and evaluate the expression.

2. List Processing

- Find distinct values to locate the second largest.
- Remove all occurrences of that value.
- Keep the original order of remaining elements.

3. Triangle Classification

- Check for validity using the triangle inequality (a + b > c).
- Determine type using the Pythagorean theorem:
- Acute (a² + b² > c²), Right (=), Obtuse (<).
- Also classify by sides: scalene, isosceles, or equilateral.

4. Quadratic Solver

- Handle special cases (a = 0 → linear).
- Compute discriminant D = b² - 4ac to determine number of roots.
- Round roots to two decimals and output in ascending order.

5. Accumulation Sequence

- Alternate signs (+, -) for each term.
- Compute powers manually using repeated multiplication.
- Sum the first 15 terms of the sequence.

6. String Sanitization

- Replace _ with spaces and remove special symbols.
- Keep only letters, digits, and single spaces.
- Capitalize each word (title case).

7. Digit Analysis

- Use % and // to check each digit.
- Count numbers containing both digits 3 and 7.
- Avoid string conversion.

8. Pig Latin with Blends

- If a word starts with a vowel, add “yay.”
- If it starts with a blend, move the blend to the end + “ay.”
- Otherwise, move the first consonant + “ay.”
- Remember common blends like sch, str, scr, thr, spl, etc.

The main operators are + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division), ** (powers), // (floor division), % (remainder). Examples: 5 - 2 = 3; 22 / 8 = 2.75; 2 ** 3 = 8. Division with / gives a float.

4. Output with print()

Use print(value) to display a value. Text goes in quotes; calculations do not. The default end of a print() call is a newline (end="\n").

# S1MPA-4 Lesson 04: Lists

## Lesson 04: Lists

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Computer Science H review guide (PA). Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

1. List Basics and Indexing

A list is an ordered, changeable collection written with square brackets. Separate the elements with commas. An index identifies an element’s position and starts at 0.

animals = ["cat", "bat", "rat", "elephant"]

print(animals[0])     # cat

print(animals[2])     # rat

print(len(animals)) # 4

print(animals[len(animals) - 1]) # elephant

2. Change, Add, and Remove Elements

Operation                     Syntax                            Effect

Replace by index              lst[1] = 10                       Changes the second element. Append at end                 lst.append(12)                    Adds one element to the end. Insert at position            lst.insert(2, 12)                 Inserts at index 2; shifts later elements. Delete by position            del lst[2]                        Removes the element at index 2. Remove by value               lst.remove(3)                     Removes the FIRST occurrence of 3. Find by value                 lst.index(7)                      Returns the FIRST matching index.

3. Trace a List

nums = [1, 3, 3, 5]

nums.remove(3)        # [1, 3, 5]

nums.insert(1, 9) # [1, 9, 3, 5]

nums[2] = 7        # [1, 9, 7, 5]

del nums[0]        # [9, 7, 5]

print(nums.index(7)) # 1

Key distinction: del uses a position, while remove() uses a value. Also, remove() and index() act on the first matching value.

4. Other List Methods Mentioned in the Exploration Task

Method               Quick meaning                           Method                 Quick meaning pop()                Remove and return an item.              sort()                 Sort the existing list. copy()               Make a shallow copy.                    sorted()               Return a new sorted list. reverse()            Reverse list in place.                  clear()                Remove all items. count(x)             Count occurrences of x.                 extend(iterable)       Add items from an iterable.

5. List References and Copies

A list variable refers to a list object in memory. When b = a, both names refer to the same list; changing an element using either name changes the list seen by both. In contrast, b = a.copy() creates a separate (shallow) list, so changes to its top-level elements do not affect a.

a = [0, 1, 2]

b = a                 # Same list, two names

a[0] = 10

print(b)              # [10, 1, 2]

b[1] = 20

print(a)              # [10, 20, 2]

b = a.copy()          # New list object

a[0] = 100

print(b)              # [10, 20, 2]

When removing elements during iteration, loop over a copy so that changing the original list does not skip items:

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]

for x in nums.copy():

if x % 2 == 0:

nums.remove(x)

print(nums)            # [1, 3]

Remember: copy() is shallow, so nested mutable objects inside the lists may still be shared.

statements
