# S1MPA-9 Lesson 09: While loops

## Lesson 09: While loops

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Computer Science H review guide (PA). Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

A program sometimes needs to repeat an action until it reaches a result. A while loop does this by checking a condition before every pass. If the condition is already false, nothing inside the loop runs. This makes while useful when you cannot know the number of repetitions in advance, such as when doubling a thickness until it reaches a target.

How the loop stops

The program needs a starting value, a condition to test, and an update inside the loop. The update matters because it can eventually make the condition false. In the paper-folding example, thickness < target is the test, and the line below doubles the current thickness after a fold.

thickness *= 2

A counter can record how many passes have happened. An accumulator serves a different purpose: it stores a result that grows with each pass. For the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n, total begins at 0, and the current number i is added each time.

total += i       # the same as total = total + i

The end of a loop is easy to misjudge by one pass. If i begins at 1 and the test is i <= 4, the loop runs with i equal to 1, 2, 3, and 4. After i increases to 5, the test is false. Without an update that can reach this point, a while loop may keep running, such as the expression while True.

# S1MPA-10 Lesson 10: String manipulation

## Lesson 10: String manipulation

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Computer Science H review guide (PA). Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

A string is text stored as a sequence of characters. Once text comes from input, it often needs cleaning or inspection before the program can use it. The methods here return a new result, so the original string stays the same unless you assign the result to a variable.

Removing characters at the ends

strip() removes whitespace such as spaces, tabs, and newlines from both ends of a string. lstrip() works only at the left end, and rstrip() only at the right. This is useful when a user types extra spaces around an answer.

"   hello   ".strip()          →   "hello"

You can also give strip() a set of characters to remove. For example, strip("-*") removes any - or * characters it finds at either end. It stops as soon as it reaches a different character. It does not remove the same characters from the middle, and the argument is not treated as one exact piece of text.

"--*Hi*--".strip("-*")             →   "Hi"

Finding and taking part of a string

Each character has an index, or position. The first position is 0, while -1 refers to the last character. len() gives the number of characters, including spaces and punctuation. Asking for a position beyond the string raises an error.

"python"[0] → "p"

"python"[-1] → "n"

"python"[10] → Error

A slice takes a range of characters. In s[start:stop], start is included and stop is left out. If either number is omitted, the slice begins at the start or continues to the end. Note that a slice can safely extend past the end of the string.

"python"[1:4]       →    "yth"

"python"[:-1]       →    "pytho"

The operators in and not in answer a yes-or-no question about whether text appears in a string. Together, these tools can clean extra symbols around a sentence or keep only the visible ends of a phone number.

"+" in "1+2"    →       True

## Lesson 11: String manipulation II

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Computer Science H review guide (PA). Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

A sentence can be easier to work with after it has been separated into words. Once the words have been changed, they can be joined into a sentence again. This lesson also adds methods for changing letter case and checking what a string contains.

Separating and joining text

split() turns one string into a list of smaller strings. With no argument, it separates at whitespace and treats a run of spaces as one gap. If you provide a delimiter, it separates at that exact character or piece of text. This difference matters when there are two spaces in a row.

("a b" contains two spaces)

"a b".split() → ["a", "b"]

"a b".split(" ") → ["a", "", "b"]

join() does the reverse: it combines strings, placing its separator between them. The separator goes before .join(), and every item being joined must itself be a string.

"-".join(["a", "b", "c"])       →   "a-b-c"

Several short operations can be chained. If url holds

"http://cn.shsid.org/img/admission_btn.png", splitting at / gives the filename as the last piece. Splitting that piece at the period then removes the extension.

url.split("/")[-1].split(".")[0]        →     "admission_btn"

Letter case and character tests

upper() makes a new uppercase string, lower() makes a lowercase one, and title() capitalizes the start of each word. The methods isupper(), islower(), and istitle() check whether a string has the corresponding case and return True or False.

"chicekn".upper()     →   "CHICEKN"

Other tests check what kinds of characters are present. isalpha() accepts letters, isdigit() accepts digits, and isalnum() accepts letters and digits together. These are useful when an input field is supposed to contain only a name or a number.

"A9".isalnum()   →    True

"A9".isalpha()   →    False

A digit does not count as an uppercase or lowercase letter, so "A9".isupper() is True because its only letter is uppercase. A string with no letters that have case does not pass isupper() or islower().

Changing a sentence word by word

The Pig Latin exercise combines split(), indexing, slices, and join(). A word starting with a vowel gains yay. If it starts with one of the listed two-letter consonant blends, those two letters move to the end before ay is added. Otherwise, only the first consonant moves. apple → appleyay, ship → ipshay, cat → atcay

# S1MPA-12 Lesson 12: Nested loops

## Lesson 12: Nested loops

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm (PA) Computer Science H review guide (PA). Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For a printed pattern, the outer loop usually moves from one row to the next. The inner loop completes the characters in the current row before the outer loop moves on. This is why the inner loop must start over for every row.

Building rows

A square with n rows has n characters in every row. A growing triangle is different: row 1 has one character, row 2 has two, and so on. A shrinking triangle starts at n characters and loses one each row. Writing down the width of each row first makes the loop bounds easier to choose.

With n = 4, a growing triangle has rows 1, 22, 333, 4444.

A centered pyramid needs spaces before the digits. On row r of n, it has n - r leading spaces and 2r - 1 copies of the row number. The widths for n = 4 are therefore 1, 3, 5, and 7. Normally print() moves to a new line. Adding end="" inside the parenthesis after the expression to be printed, i.e. print(“Hello world!”, end="") keeps the next character on the same line, and a plain print() after the inner loop finishes the row. The escape sequence \n can also put a newline inside a string.

Patterns based on positions

The X pattern depends on where a character lies, not just how wide a row is. With rows and columns numbered from 0, one o appears where the column matches the row; the other lies at its mirror position, n - 1 - row. Every other position is +. The exercise asks for an odd width, so an even input must be requested again.

The final exercise checks perfect numbers. A number is perfect when its smaller positive divisors add up to the number itself: 6 = 1 + 2 + 3. Checking each candidate through 1000 gives 6, 28, and 496.

Choosing a tool from the task

A task may need more than one route through this chart. For example, changing every word in a sentence uses text methods to separate and join the words, plus a loop to visit them one at a time.

Example programs

Here are some complete examples of the smaller ideas above. The comments point out steps that are easy to overlook, such as changing a loop variable, handling zero, or choosing which part of a string to keep.

Counting folds and adding values

The paper starts at 0.05 mm. Everest’s height is 8,848.13 m, which is 8,848,130 mm. Using the same unit on both sides of the comparison lets the loop stop as soon as the paper is thick enough.

thickness = 0.05

target = 8848130 # millimeters

folds = 0

while thickness < target:

thickness *= 2 # one fold doubles the thickness

folds += 1      # count that fold

print(folds, thickness)

The result is 28 folds and 13,421,772.8 mm. A running sum uses the same starting-test-update structure. Here, int() turns the input text into a number, while total stores the sum so far.

n = int(input())

i = 1

total = 0

while i <= n:

total += i # include the current number

i += 1       # move to the next number

print(total)

The fraction sequence begins at 2/1, then continues 3/2, 5/3, and so on. The next numerator is the sum of the current pair, while the next denominator is the old numerator. The assignment to a and b happens together, so both new values use the old pair.

a, b = 2, 1

total = 0

for _ in range(20): # repeat for 20 terms

total += a / b

a, b = a + b, a # build the next fraction

print(f"{total:.3f}")

The underscore is just a loop variable whose value is not needed. The final line shows three digits after the decimal point, giving 32.660.

Converting between bases

To read a number written in base 2 through 9, process its digits from left to right. Each new digit shifts the previous value one place by multiplying it by the base, then adds the digit. The code assumes the digits entered belong to the chosen base.

base = int(input("Base (2-9): "))

digits = input("Number: ")

value = 0

for digit in digits:

value = value * base + int(digit)      # shift, then add

print(value)

For example, binary 1010 produces decimal 10. Going the other direction uses remainders. Each remainder is the next rightmost digit, so str() turns it into text and places it at the front of the answer. Integer division with //= then removes that place. The last line also handles an input of zero.

base = int(input("Base (2-9): "))

number = int(input("Decimal number: "))

answer = ""

while number > 0:

answer = str(number % base) + answer # add a digit at the front

number //= base # remove the place just converted

print(answer or "0")

Cleaning and changing text

In the first example, strip() removes the surrounding spaces, then strip("-*") removes the dashes and asterisks. Neither call changes text in the middle. The phone number stays a string so its first and last three digits can be sliced. Two asterisks stand in for the five hidden digits in the lesson’s display format.

text = " ----***Hi!***---- "

print(text.strip().strip("-*")) # Hi!

phone = "13112345306"

print(phone[:3] + "**" + phone[-3:]) # 131**306

For a sentence with different kinds of symbols at its ends, the same idea can be extended by locating its first and last letter, then slicing between them. That leaves punctuation inside the sentence in place.

This Pig Latin program uses the lesson’s list of two-letter blends. It first makes the sentence lowercase and splits it into words. enumerate() supplies both the word and its position in the list, allowing the changed word to replace the original. The example assumes a nonempty sentence of alphabetic words.

blends = {"sh", "gl", "ch", "ph", "tr", "br", "fr",

"bl", "gr", "st", "sl", "cl", "pl", "fl"}

words = input().lower().split()

for i, word in enumerate(words):

if word[0] in "aeiou":

words[i] = word + "yay"

elif word[:2] in blends: # check two letters before one

words[i] = word[2:] + word[:2] + "ay"

else:

words[i] = word[1:] + word[0] + "ay"

print(" ".join(words)) # put spaces back between words

Reading a student record

A line such as John 9(3) 178 has three fields: name, grade with class in parentheses, and height. split() separates the fields. Splitting 9(3) at ( leaves 9 and 3), so the final character of the second piece must be removed to get the class number.

parts = input().split()

valid = len(parts) == 3

if valid:

name, group, height = parts

pieces = group.split("(") # grade and class with ")"

valid = (len(pieces) == 2 and group.count(")") == 1

and group.endswith(")") and name.isalpha()

and height.isdigit() and pieces[0].isdigit()

and pieces[1][:-1].isdigit())

if valid:

print(f"stu1 name: {name}, grade: {pieces[0]}, "

f"class: {pieces[1][:-1]}, height: {height}")

else:

print("Error")

The tests require a letter-only name, a digit-only height, and one valid pair of parentheses. If a test fails, the output is Error; John 9(3) 178 produces stu1 name: John, grade: 9, class: 3, height: 178.

Printing a growing triangle

The outer loop chooses rows 1 through n. Since range() stops before its second number, the code uses n + 1 to include row n. The inner loop prints the row number once per position; end="" keeps the digits together, and the final print() moves to the next row.

n = int(input())

for row in range(1, n + 1):

for col in range(row):

print(row, end="") # stay on this row

print() # start the next row

**L16 Dictionary**

A dictionary is a collection of **key-value pairs**, where each key is **unique** and maps to a specific value. We create a dictionary by enclosing a comma-separated list of key-value pairs within curly braces {}. Each key is separated form its value by a colon (key:value), e.g. {1:’a’, 2:’b’, 3:’c’}

**Dictionary VS List**

- Dictionary use {} while list use []
- Dictionary access values through d[key], while list access through lst[idx]
- Dictionary adding and modifying element using d[key] = value, while the list adding the element through suffix (append/insert), and modifying element with lst[idx] = element.

**L17 Comments**

**L18 Files and File Path**

**Path**

A path refers to the location of a file on a computer. Different operating systems use different path formats, as shown below:

- Windows: C:\path\to\file
- Linux: /path/to/file

There are two kinds of paths: absolute paths and relative paths. Both describe the route from a specific directory to a target file. The difference is that an absolute path starts from the root directory (e.g., C:\ or /) and continues all the way to the file. A relative path starts from the current working directory and points to the target location, typically written as .\path\to\file. If you want to start searching from the parent directory, you can use two dots: ..\the\path\to\file. You can think of .. as “go back to the parent directory” before continuing.

In the examples above, path, to, and file can be considered different levels (directory layers). For example, in /path/to/file, path is level 1, to is level 2, and so on.

**Slashes**

**L19 Computer Color**

All colors we generated form the three spectral hues of Red, Green, and Blue, which aligned with the color receptors in out eye. In specific, by using 3 decimal numbers, we can identify a certain color in computer by RGB. The range of the numbers is 0-255, includes 256 levels. We can use (R, G, B) to represent the color in denary.

By the way, there are to more abnormal ways to represent colors: Binary and Hexadecimal.

**Binary in Computer Color**

In binary we contains only 0 and 1 as digits. In this mode, we have to use 24 numbers to represent one color (8 numbers for each primary color), e.g. we use 11111111 11111111 11111111 to represent white color.

**Hexadecimal**

Since the binary representations are usually hard to read, programmers found a lazy way to represent, which is hexadecimal.

Each digit in hexadecimal contains 16 different numbers (1-9 and a-f which represents numbers greater than 9)

By using hexadecimal, we can condense 4digits of binary number to 1digit of hexadecimal. E.g. to represent white color, we use #FFFFFF.

**CMYK**

CMYK is the standard color model for printing. It represents a color by specifying the amounts of four inks: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Black. Unlike RGB, which is an additive model used for screens (white at 255,255,255): the increase of RGB ink on white paper reduces the light reflected to eyes, making colors appear dark. Therefore, CMYK (white at 0,0,0) is used in print workflows, to control ink coverage and achieve accurate printed colors.

**L20 Number System**

In everyday life, we usually use the decimal (base10) system (0, 1, 2, …, 9). However, other counting systems are also used in specific contexts—for example, timekeeping uses units based on 60 (60 seconds per minute and 60 minutes per hour), and “a dozen” is based on 12. In computers, processors are built from countless transistors, each of which has two states (on and off). Therefore, binary (base2) is used to represent data and instructions at a low level: 0 represents off and 1 represents on. Hexadecimal (base16) is often used as a convenient shorthand for binary because one hex digit corresponds to four bits.

**Binary**

As mentioned earlier, computers represent data at a low level using binary: **0** indicates off and **1** indicates on. Each 0/1 digit is a **binary digit**, called a **bit** (**b**).

**Base Conversion (Search online for detailed steps)**

| Conversion | Method |
|---|---|
| Binary → Decimal | Sum each bit × ${2}^{\text{pos}}$ (position starts at 0 from right). |
| Binary → Hex | Group bits into 4 from the right, convert each group to one hex-digit |
| Hex → Binary | Replace each hex-digit with 4-bits binary, then concatenate. |
| Hex → Decimal | Sum each digit value × ${16}^{\text{pos}}$ (position starts at 0 from right). |
| Decimal → Binary | Repeatedly divide by 2, record remainders, read remainders bottom-up. |
| Decimal → Hex | Repeatedly divide by 16, record remainders (0–F), read remainders bottom-up |

**Data**

When we store each binary digit, we can treat it as data. Starting from a **byte** (8 bits), storage units are commonly scaled by **1024 (2¹⁰)**.

**Bitwise Operation**

a fast, low-level computer function that manipulates individual bits (0s and 1s) within binary numbers, performing logical tasks like AND, OR, XOR, and shifts, directly on their binary representations.

| Operator | Syntax | Description (In Binary) |
|---|---|---|
| AND | a&b | 1 only where both bits are 1 |
| OR | a\|b | 1 where either bit is 1 |
| XOR | a^b | 1 where bits differ (0/1 or 1/0) |
| Left Shift | a<<n | Shift bits left by n; equals a * (2**n) |
| Right Shift | a>>n | Shift bits right by n; equals a // (2**n) for non-negative ints |

print(“Not A”)

If-elif-else statement

- Structure:

if condition1:

statements1

elif condition2:

statements2

else:

statements3

Example:

age = int(input("What is your age? "))

if age < 11:

print("You are kid.")

elif age < 20:

print("You are teenager.")

else:

print("You are adult.")

While Loop

- Repeats the command inside the loop until the condition is satisfied.

- Structure

while condition:

statements

- Example:

i,s = 1,0

n = int(input("Enter n: "))

while i <= n:

s += i

i += 1

print(s)

- This will add all of the integers from 1 to n (taken from the user’s input).

Number systems

- These are systems of digits used for mathematical operations.

- Decimal: The system that we use every day.

- Binary: Only has 2 digits, 0 and 1

- Hexadecimal: based on 16, ranges from 0-9 and A-F (A, B, C, D, E, F represent the five numbers 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, respectively)

- Octal numeral system: based on 8; digits range from 0-7.

- These systems’ place values are represented by their powers. For example, with decimal, we have ones digits (10^0), tens digits (10^1), hundreds digits(10^2), etc.

- The number 1234 is equal to 1 x 10^3 + 2 x 10^2 + 3 x 10^1 + 4 x 10^0.

- In a similar way with base two, 10110 is equal to 1 x 2^4 + 0 x 2^3 + 1 x 2^2 +

1 x 2^1 + 0 x 2^0 = 20 when converted to base-10.

- Conversion: This is one of the hardest points for our class.
- To convert from decimal to another number system, you divide the given

decimal number by the other number system’s base (whichever number that

system is named after, e.g., base-2, aka binary, will be 2) over and over until

the quotient is 0. Then, look at the final remainder and all of the earlier

remainders from the bottom up and read them in order to find the final

number in the new base.

- Let’s set an example.

- A number has a value of 10 in decimal. To convert this number to

base-2, we will divide it repeatedly until the quotient is zero. 10 / 2 = 5

R 0, 5 / 2 = 2 R 1, 2 / 2 = 1 R 0, and 1 / 2 = 0 R 1. Then, we just look

at the remainders. 1, 0, 1, 0. This becomes 1010 in binary.

- To convert from another system to decimal, we want to use the example we

mentioned earlier about place values. Simply find the place value and multiply

it by the number in that place, and then add up the values to find the final

value of the number in decimal.

- Say, for example, we are given the binary number 1010. To convert it

to decimal, we need to find the place values first. The first 1 has a

place value of 2^3 because there are three places to the right of it,

and the rest follow an identical property. Then, we just multiply the

values of the digits by the place values and add them. 1 x 2^3 + 0 x

2^2 + 1 x 2^1 + 0 x 2^0 = 10, and that is our decimal value.

Bits and bytes:

- Bit: One “0” or “1” in a binary system, represented as “b”

- Byte: A group of 8 bits, represented as “B”

- Larger storage units:

- On the left side, 1000 kilobytes = 1megabyte

- On the right side, 1024 kibibytes = 1mebibyte

- 1 kilobyte = 1000 bytes

- 1 kibibyte = 1024 bytes

String Manipulation

- s.strip(str) removes all characters in the string str from the beginning and end of

string s.

- If s = ‘…..abc….’ then s.strip(.) returns ‘abc’.

- The generalized form is .strip(), which removes all whitespace characters (including spaces, tabs, and newlines).

- .lstrip() and .rstrip() are variants that only remove all characters in the parentheses from one side of the string, either the left or the right.

- Strings, just like lists, have indexes. From our earlier example, str[0] = ‘.’, and str[5] = ‘a’.

- in checks to see if the value before the operator is in the list or string after the operator.

- x in s returns True if x is in s, and False if not.

- in works even if only part of the value is in the given list or string. For

example, ‘John’ in nameList where nameList = “…, Johnson, …” returns True.

- len(str) returns the length of string str, including whitespace characters.

- String slicing

- Removes the specified parts from a string

- Syntax: str[start slice:end slice]

- start slice and end slice stand for the beginning and ending index positions of

the slice (end slice non-inclusive).

- If str = ‘Python’, then str[1:4] returns ‘yth’.

- The start slice defaults to 0 and the end slice defaults to the end of the string.

- str[:-1] returns an empty string.

- str[:1] returns only the first character, str[-1:] returns only the last character.

Common Misconceptions and Mistakes

- Data types can be very finicky. People will often forget to take into account the differences between integers and strings when coding.

- Most notably, with the print function, you should almost always convert between data types with the int() or str() functions

- For example, if you have defined variable a = 3, then print(a + 1) will print 4. However, if a is a string, say a = ‘3’, then print(a + 1) will be an error because

you can’t add an integer to a string. Additionally, print(‘a + 1’) will print a + 1

without running calculations, and print(‘a’ + ‘1’) will return ‘a1’

- Furthermore, if you have defined a = ‘Hello’ and b = 1 and are trying to print a string, then you must use either addition or a comma to add the two. print(a +

b) directly will fail, but print(a + str(b)) or print(a, b) will print Hello1 (which will

be a string data type). Notice how using a comma does not require

converting b to a string, while using addition does.

- int() has an interesting quirk where, if the string contains a float number, there will be an error.

- What I mean by this is that if you try the command int(‘4.0’), the command will return an error.

- However, if you use float(‘4.0’) or float(‘4’), it will still run properly.
- When printing with print(“…”), the quotation marks will be removed.
- When using for loops, if a range() function is used, then the “i” in the “for i in range(…)” will be defined by the range function. However, if the “i” is used in “for i in

a” when a is either a list or a string, then i will be defined by a, iterating through each

item/character in a by order of index, not value.

# S1F-1 2.1 Computer Colors

## 2.1 Computer Colors

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final Computer Science S review guide (PA). Writers: Leona 9-7. Editor: Max Zheng 9-1. Range: CH2-CH3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

- A computer’s primary colors are **red, green and blue**
  - all colors we generate form the three spectral hues of red, green and blue
  - CMYK: proper reference for printed color
- HSV/HSL/HSI
  - H: Hue -> the pure dominant color (original colorness)
  - S: Saturation -> intensity/purity of a color
  - V: Value -> lightness or darkness
  - L: Lightness -> color’s brightness (amount of black/white)
  - I: Intensity -> brightness or dullness of a color
- Binary notation of colors: 24 numbers to represent a color
  - EG: 111111 111111 111111 is white
  - The first 6 “1”s represent the red part of the color, the next group of “1”s represent the green part and the last group of “1”s represent the blue part
- Hexadecimal: using 6 letters/numbers to represent a color
  - EG: #FF FF FF represents white
  - The first group of “F”s represent the red part, the second group represents green, and the third group represents blue
- Ways to store characters:
  - **Morse code**: the use of dots and dashes. This can be uneffective as letters can be mixed up
  - ASC II: developed from telegraph codes, encodes 128 specified characters into **7-bit integers**
  - Uppercase and lowercase letters have different numeric values (e.g., 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97)
- Graphic formats can be formatted in:
  - GIF, shows 256 kinds of colors at most in one picture
  - JPEG: millions of kidns of colors (28*28*28=16777216), saves memory space in computer
  - PNG: combines advantages of GIF and JPEG, good quality, can be transparent, not very popular as many web pages cannot show pictures in this format
  - BMP/RLE: one of the most popular formats used to save images on windows operating system
  - PSD: used in photoshop, save all detailed elements made in photoshop such as layers, color modes, path and channel etc, occupy large memory in computer but can be compressed
  - HEIF: supports multiple bit depths, depending on the encoder and use case, memory is about 50% smaller than the JPEG format, shows billions of colors (230), records images with richer information, compatibility is limited
- bit depth: color depth per chennel, not the total file size or container overhead

## 2.2 Digital Graphics

- An image created/edited on a computer is either a bitmapped or vector graphic
  - **Bitmapped**: AKA raster graphics, consists of pixels, if you enlarge a bitmap you enlarge a pixel
    - pixels become more obvious and image loses cripsness and clarity
  - **Vector**: uses mathematical formulas to define lines, curves and other attributes of digital images
    - you use vector graphics editing program
    - Vector files are generally much smaller than bitmapped
- The number of **pixel per inch** (ppi) determines the resolution of bitmap grapics
  - photo display on a computer screen usually looks realistic at 72 ppi
  - vector graphics do not rely on resolution for clarity, but its’ display on a computer screen does
- **color depth**: in graphic files and applications, color depth refers to the number of distinct colors an image can contain/how many bits per pixel
  - EG 24-bit image has color depth of 16.7 million colors, called **full color imag**
- **Field of View/Field of vision (FOV):** extent of observable world that is seen at any given moment
  - Humans have ≈210 degree of forward facing horizontal arc of their visual field’
  - vertical range of the visual field in humans is around 150 degrees
  - some birds have complete/nearly complete 360 degree FOV
- **Aspect ratio**: relationship between its width and height
  - expressed as (x,y)
  - common aspect ratios: 5:4, 4:3, 16:10, 16:9
- Brief history
  - **2003:** most computer monitors had 4:3 aspect ratio, some had 5:4
  - **2003-2006**: 16:10 became common in laptops and standalone monitors
  - **2008**: industry moved from 4:3 and 16:10 to 16:9 as the standard ratio
  - **2010**: All monitors and laptops moved to 16:9 aspect ratio
  - **2011**: 16:9 reso of 1920*1080 became popular among steam users
  - **2012**: resolution became 1366*768

## 2.3 Alpha Channel

- **alpha compositing**: process of combining an image with a background to create the appearance of partial or full transparency
  - keep an associate matte for each element
  - In a 2D image element, which stores a color for each pixel, additional data is stored in the alpha channel with a value between 0 and 1
    - 0 means pixel does not have any coverage info and is transparent
    - 1 means the pixel is opaque because the geometry overlapped the pixel
  - one more number is required to store **alpha**
    - from (148,255,255) to (148,255,255,0)
      - first 3 numbers imply the color
      - last three imply the alpha
- if three primary colors share the same number, this color contains only brightness, it can only be black, white or gray
  - (0,0,0) is black
  - (255,255,255) is white
  - (100,100,100) is gray
- **premultiplied alpha**: if the alpha channel is used in an image, its common to alsp multiply the color by the alpha value
  - saves space
  - **linear interpolation**: riven two red points, the blue line is the linear interpolate between the points, and then value y at x may be found using this method

## 2.4 Computer monitors

- **computer monitors**: the size of a display is usually given by monitor manufacturers based on the diagonal
  - measure in unit inch
  - display devices: cathode ray tube (CRT), liquid crytal display(LCD), organic light-emitting diode (OLED)
    - **CRT**: old fashioned, vacuum tube containing an electron gun and phosphorescent screen used to view images
    - **LCD:** most common, has diffraction grating, crystal and backlight
    - **OLED:** monitor of the future, simple structure, self emissive

## 2.5 Image Compression

- **uncompressed image - raw file**: captured by a digital camera or scanner’s scensors, this captures a high level of image detail, with large file sizes and losslessquality
  - direct image data means you start with a high-quality image that can be edited, converted and compressed in a non-destructive manner
- **lossy vs lossless**
  - lossless: oreferred for archival purposes, for medical imaging, technical drawings, clip art, comics
  - lossy: suitable for natural images EG photographs in applications
- **lossless compression**
  - Run-length encoding (RLE) is a simple form of data compression where runs of data are stored as a single data value and count, rather than as the original run
    - example of RLE: W representing white and B representing black: WWWWWBWW
    - instead this can be compressed into 5W1B2W
  - Differential pulse-code modulation (DPCM) encodes the changes between consecutive samples of a signal rather than the signal’s value directly
    - reduces the bit rate
    - input can be an analog signal or digital signal
    - methods of encoding:
      - quantize the samples, output is the difference between the current and previous sample
      - quantize the difference between the current sample and output of a local decoder
    - color spaced is reduced to the most common colots, these selected colors are defined in a color palette stored within the mage harder
      - each pixel references the index of its corresponding color in the palette
      - this approach can be combined with dithering to minimize posterization artifacts
  - **entropy encoding**:
    - **Huffman coding**: separating the input into component symbols and replacing each with a code, uses variable length codes to represent different characters
      - shorter codes -> assigned to more frequently occuring characters and longer to less frequent ones, results in compressed data representation
      - optimal for minimizing the total number of bits used
    - **Arithmetic coding**: encoding the entire message into a single number, a fraction n where (0≤n≤1)
  - **chroma subsampling**: human eye perceives spatial changes of brightness more sharply than color, so this method averages/drops some of the chominance info in the image
  - **transform coding:** most commonly used method, Fourier related transform such as the **discrete cosine transform (DCT)** is widely used
    - wavelet transform is also used extensively, followed by quantization and entropy coding

# S1F-2 3.1 Frame Rate

## 3.1 Frame Rate

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final Computer Science S review guide (PA). Writers: Leona 9-7. Editor: Max Zheng 9-1. Range: CH2-CH3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

- **Video: fast switching pictures**
  - Frame rate: AKA frame frequency/frames per second (FPS); the frequence at which an imaging device produces unique consecutive images called frames
  - unit: FPS, Hz(Hertz)
  - threshold of human visual perception: 24 fps
- Standard frame rates in cinema/TV: 24 fps(cinematic films), 25 fps(PAL(Asia), SECAM(Europe)), 30 fps(NTSC, North America).
- 24 fps: progressive format, transferring video signal to film (fps of film: 23.976)
- 48 fps: progressive format trialed in the film industry, reduce motion blur and flicker, EG “THe Hobbit”
- 50 or 60 fps: HDTV/video in high definition based on 25 and 30 fps

## 3.2 Data Rate and Bandwidth

- Stream: sequence of data elements made available over time
  - divides a video into several parts, which are transported one by one, while one part is playing the next is being loaded
- Bandwidth: measurement of bit-rate of available or consumed data communication resources expressed in bits per second or multiples of it
- Data rate: speed of stream transmission
  - decides how much data will be transported each second
  - Conversion:
    - 1 TB = 1024 GB
    - 1 GB = 1024 Mbps
    - 1 Mbps = 1024 Kbps (Kilobyte)
    - 1 Kbps = 1024 Byte
    - 1 Byte = 8 bit
  - Data rate = File size (bit) / length of file (sec)
  - unit of data rate and bandwidth are both bps (bits per second)
  - data rate is determined by: screen size, frame rate, and codec
    - data rte of SD vid: around 512 KB-2M
    - data rate of 720P vid: 4MB-16MB
    - data rate of 1080 vid: 8MB-48MB
  - Bandwidth of our internet connection should be larger than the data rate of video

**3.3. 3D Vision**

- 3D vision: we see two 2D images separately with out left and right eye, our brain combines them and gives a 3D depth
- **Anaglyph 3D:**
  - stereoscopic 3D effect achieved by means of encoding each eye’s image using filters of different colors, typically red and cyan
  - contain two differently filtered colored images, one for each eye
  - color filters to create 3D effect, eg. red-cyan color filters
- **Polarization 3D system:**
  - polarization glasses to create the illusion of 3D images by restricting the light that reaches each eye
  - low-cost eyeglasses which contain a pair of different polarizing filters
  - two images are projected superimposed the same screen or display through different polarizing filters
  - linear polarizer converts an unpolarized beam into one with a single linear polarization:
    - vertical components of all waves are transmitted
    - horizontal components are absorbed and reflected
- **Active Shutter 3D system:**
  - openly presenting the image intended for the left eye while blocking the right eye’s view, then presenting the right0eye’s image while blocking the left eye
  - this is repeated rapidly so that the interruptions do not interfere with the perceived fusion of the two images into a single 3D image
  - EG NVIDIA 3D vision system
- **HUD:**
  - Head mounted display (HMD): display device worn on the head/part of a helmet, has a small display optic in front of one or each eye
  - EG Google Glasses

## 3.4 Video Compression

- **Uncompressed**: stores every single data of a video, both useful and useless
  - loses no quality during the process of editing or copying from one form of media into another
- **video compression**: encoding or decoding a digital data strean or signal
  - **lossless**: used for archiving data in a compressed form while retaining all the information present in the orginal stream
  - **lossy**: reduce quality by some amount in order to achieve compression, formats include mpeg, mov, mkv
  - **encoder/decoder**: used in multi-media area for video compression and decompression
  - **codec and format**: old time codec and format are strongly related, even the players are related to the codecs
  - usually format and codec are in pairs, but not always
    - sometimes we cannot open a video with one format while another video with this format can be opened
  - **container format**: special video format that allowed the users to encode videos with different codecs but sharing the same format name or extension
    - eg. AVI, QuickTime(MOV), Mpeg4 etc
    - contain different codecs but allows users to encode audio/vid with different compressors

    - Audio support:

## 3.5 Video Connectors

- **Video connectors**: electric connectors for carrying video signal, of either analog or digital format
  - both analog and digital signals are used with some styles of connectors, knowledge of the interface used is necessary for a successful signal transmission
  - some interface types use only a distinctive connectors or family of connectors to ensure compatibility
- **VGA**(Video Graphic Array): three-row 15-pin connector, the 15-pin VGA connector is found on many video cards, computer monitors, and high definition TV sets
  - same VGA cable can be used with a variety of supported VGA resolutions
  - ranging from 640*350 px at 70 Hz to 1280*1024 px at 85 Hz and up to 2048*1536 px at 85 Hz
  - 25 MB/s
- **DVI(**Digital Visual Interface**):** designed to transmit uncompressed digital video, can be configured to support multiple modes, DVI-D, DVI-A, or DVI-I
  - Digital vid stream: 1920*1200 at 60 Hz - 2560*1600 at 60 Hz
  - Analog vid stream: 1920*1200 at 60 Hz
  - 7.92 Gbits/s
- **HDMI**: Proprietary audio/video interface for transferring uncompressed video data and compressed or uncompressed digital audio data
  - 2.25 GB/s
- **Thunderbolt**: 40 Gbits/s

## 3.6 Storage Devices

- **Magnetic storage**: uses different patterns of magnetisation in a magnetisable material to store data is a form of non-volatile memory
  - Analog recording
  - Digital recording: floppy disk, hard disk
- **Optical storage**: optical disc is a flat, usually circular disc which encodes binary data in the form of pits (0) and lands (1) on a spcial material (aluminum) on one of its flat surface
  - CD, DVD, HD DVD, Blue-Ray
- **Flash storage**: electron non-volatile computer storage medium that can be electrically erased and reprogrammed
  - memory cards
  - USB flash drives
  - solid0state drives (SSD)
